question: What proportion of adults with cirrhosis without hepatitis B have an ultrasound (with or without alpha-fetoprotein) for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance at least every 6 months?
why: Late detection of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in cirrhosis loses the window for curative treatment. Surveillance interval is rarely measured directly in the library; the closest related audit found only 9% liver imaging and 8% alpha-fetoprotein testing in a comparable surveillance population [7348]. No closed-loop audit of 6-monthly HCC surveillance timing in cirrhosis has been published in the library.

standard.wording: Offer ultrasound (with or without measurement of serum alpha-fetoprotein) every 6 months as surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) for people with cirrhosis who do not have hepatitis B virus infection.

population: Adults with a coded diagnosis of cirrhosis (any cause other than hepatitis B) under hepatology follow-up who have had at least 2 surveillance scans. Exclude patients on end-of-life/palliative care and those with hepatitis B.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with cirrhosis on the hepatology HCC surveillance list, looking at their last 2 scheduled scans.
data_source: Hepatology surveillance database or clinic letters for the diagnosis and surveillance list; radiology system (PACS/RIS) for ultrasound dates; biochemistry system for alpha-fetoprotein dates.

template.note: Calculated: months between the two scans

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Put every eligible patient on a single electronic 6-monthly HCC surveillance recall list (radiology or hepatology database) that books the next scan automatically when one is reported, instead of relying on the clinician to remember to re-request.
reaudit: Repeat at 6 months using the same recall list and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology or gastroenterology clinical governance meeting; if the recall list works, hand ownership to the hepatology administrative team as standard practice.
evidence: [7348] end-organ liver surveillance: liver imaging done in only 9% and alpha-fetoprotein in 8% despite a surveillance recommendation, showing surveillance intervals are not reliably met without a system
no audit in the library measures 6-monthly HCC surveillance interval adherence directly
pitfalls: Scans done elsewhere (private, another trust) are missed on PACS search: cross-check with the patient at clinic.
Small numbers if the surveillance list is short: pool 2-3 clinics.
Definition of 'on surveillance' can drift between cycles: fix the inclusion list before cycle 1.
Patients who died or transplanted in the interval should be excluded, not counted as failures.
A recall list only helps if someone actions the alert: name an owner.
pearls: Ask the hepatology secretary or specialist nurse to hold the surveillance list; they are often the best placed to run the recall.
Agree the definition of 'surveillance patient' (cirrhosis, not palliative, no transplant) with the consultant before starting.
Link AFP requesting to the same recall so both come as one task.
Re-audit before the surveillance list changes hands with rotation, and write the SOP into the department induction pack.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from PACS and the hepatology database
pass: The interval between the patient's last two surveillance ultrasound scans is 6 months or less (allowing up to 8 weeks' slippage), and this is documented in the hepatology follow-up record.

question: What proportion of adults newly diagnosed with cirrhosis are offered an upper GI endoscopy to look for oesophageal varices, unless already planned on carvedilol or propranolol?
why: Undetected varices carry a high first-bleed mortality. No audit in the library measures whether screening endoscopy is offered at the point of cirrhosis diagnosis; the nearest related work only measured endoscopy timing after a bleed had already happened [2283], [2744].

standard.wording: After a diagnosis of cirrhosis, offer the person an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to detect oesophageal varices unless they are planning to take carvedilol or propranolol to prevent decompensation.

population: Adults with a new diagnosis of cirrhosis (any cause) in the last 12 months, identified from the hepatology new-patient list or MDT. Exclude patients who already had a variceal screen for another indication.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new cirrhosis diagnosis over the last 6-12 months.
data_source: Hepatology clinic letters and MDT outcome for the diagnosis date; endoscopy reporting system for the OGD; drug chart/GP record for carvedilol or propranolol.

template.note: Pass criterion, unless beta-blocker chosen instead

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'variceal screen or beta-blocker' prompt to the new-cirrhosis MDT outcome template, which auto-generates either an endoscopy referral or a carvedilol-initiation plan before the patient leaves the meeting.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months with the next 40 new diagnoses on the same template.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology MDT; embed the outcome template as the default new-cirrhosis pathway if it works.
evidence: [2283] a district general hospital audit of upper GI bleeding found gaps in structured bleed-risk management, showing variceal risk is not systematically tracked before a bleed occurs
no audit in the library measures screening endoscopy uptake at the point of cirrhosis diagnosis
pitfalls: Patients diagnosed with cirrhosis incidentally (e.g. on imaging for another reason) can be missed from the hepatology new-patient list: cross-check radiology reports too.
Endoscopy waiting lists can push the true 6-month window out: record the referral date as well as the scan date.
Counting a beta-blocker started for another reason (e.g. hypertension) as meeting the standard is a common error: it must be started for this indication.
Losing patients to follow-up before the scan is done should be recorded, not silently excluded.
pearls: Agree with endoscopy in advance that new-cirrhosis referrals get a 'surveillance' priority code so they are not queued behind routine OGDs.
Have the MDT coordinator flag every new cirrhosis diagnosis in real time rather than searching retrospectively.
Present early results to the endoscopy unit, since they control the main bottleneck.
Keep the same 6-month reporting window across cycles so trends are comparable.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from clinic letters and the endoscopy system
pass: Within 6 months of a new cirrhosis diagnosis, the patient either has an upper GI endoscopy looking for varices, or a documented decision to start carvedilol/propranolol instead.

question: Of adults having a surveillance upper GI endoscopy for cirrhosis in whom medium or large oesophageal varices are found, what proportion have endoscopic variceal band ligation performed at the same procedure?
why: A second procedure to treat varices found at screening means a second sedation, a second bowel-prep-equivalent and a delay during which the patient can bleed. No audit in the library measures same-session banding at variceal screening.

standard.wording: Consider simultaneous endoscopic variceal band ligation if medium or large varices are detected during upper gastrointestinal endoscopy.

population: Adults having a surveillance (not emergency) OGD for varices in cirrhosis, in whom medium or large varices are found. Exclude emergency bleeds.
sample: All surveillance OGDs with medium/large varices found over 3-6 months (expect 15-30 cases in most endoscopy units).
data_source: Endoscopy reporting system (e.g. Unisoft/Endobase) for the procedure and findings; endoscopist's report for whether banding was done and why not, if omitted.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: List which endoscopists are trained in variceal band ligation on the surveillance-list booking screen, so surveillance OGDs for cirrhosis are only booked with a banding-trained endoscopist, or with rescue banding equipment and a second operator on standby.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the endoscopy unit's quality meeting and the hepatology MDT; if it works, fix the booking rule as unit policy.
evidence: no audit in the library measures same-session banding at variceal surveillance endoscopy
pitfalls: Numbers will be small in a single centre; consider a longer collection window or combining with a neighbouring unit.
Endoscopist availability for banding is a genuine, recordable constraint, not a data-collection failure: capture it as a reason, not a blank.
Distinguish surveillance procedures from emergency bleeds, which follow a different pathway and should not be pooled.
A drop in banding rates after a trained endoscopist leaves or retires needs a rota fix, not just re-teaching.
pearls: Agree the criteria for 'trained in banding' with the endoscopy lead before cycle 1.
Build the booking rule into the endoscopy referral form so it happens automatically rather than depending on memory.
Track which endoscopists most often defer banding, to target support rather than blanket teaching.
Keep the beta-blocker-instead option visible in the template, since NICE treats banding and beta-blockade as alternatives, not banding as mandatory.
effort: ~15 min per case from the endoscopy report
pass: If medium or large varices are found at a surveillance OGD, band ligation is performed in the same procedure, or a documented reason is given for not doing so (for example, no trained endoscopist available).

question: What proportion of adults with cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension (medium/large varices or ascites) are offered carvedilol or propranolol to prevent decompensation?
why: Primary prevention of decompensation with a non-selective beta-blocker is a 2023 addition to NICE guidance that is not yet embedded in most cirrhosis pathways; no audit in the library measures its uptake.

standard.wording: For people who have cirrhosis and confirmed, or suspected, clinically significant portal hypertension (for example, as indicated by a hepatic venous pressure gradient of more than 10 mmHg or the presence of oesophageal varices), consider the following options for the primary prevention of decompensation: carvedilol as the first-choice treatment ... or propranolol as the second-choice treatment, if carvedilol is contraindicated.

population: Adults with cirrhosis and documented varices (any size) or ascites, seen in hepatology clinic in the last 6 months. Exclude those already on a beta-blocker for another indication only if not explicitly for this purpose.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with cirrhosis and varices or ascites seen in hepatology outpatients.
data_source: Clinic letters and drug chart/GP shared record for the prescription; endoscopy/imaging reports for evidence of portal hypertension.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'clinically significant portal hypertension: carvedilol/propranolol offered? yes/no/why not' field to the hepatology clinic template, triggered whenever varices or ascites are coded in the notes.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same template and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology governance meeting; embed the clinic template field if uptake improves.
evidence: no audit in the library measures uptake of beta-blockers for primary prevention of decompensation in cirrhosis
pitfalls: This is a 2023 recommendation: some clinicians may not yet know it applies beyond variceal bleeding prevention, so expect a low baseline and plan teaching alongside the template.
Carvedilol needs caution in severe hepatic impairment (see the related safe-prescribing audit): don't count inappropriate starts as passes.
Distinguishing 'clinically significant' portal hypertension from cirrhosis in general needs a clear, agreed definition before data collection starts.
Heart rate/blood pressure intolerance stopping the drug should be recorded as a valid reason, not a failure.
pearls: Pair this audit with the safe-prescribing check (avoid carvedilol in severe hepatic impairment) so the same data collection covers both.
Brief the hepatology team on the 2023 change before cycle 1 so the low baseline reflects true practice, not confusion about the recommendation.
Use a pharmacist to help identify eligible patients from the clinic list in advance.
Track discontinuation rates at re-audit, since tolerability is the main barrier.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass: Carvedilol (first choice) or propranolol (if carvedilol contraindicated) is prescribed, or a documented reason is given for not offering either, in patients with cirrhosis and evidence of clinically significant portal hypertension.

question: What proportion of adults with compensated cirrhosis under hepatology follow-up have a MELD score calculated at least every 6 months?
why: A rising MELD score is the main early warning of deterioration in compensated cirrhosis, but there is no audit in the library of whether it is actually calculated at the recommended interval.

standard.wording: Calculate the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score every 6 months for people with compensated cirrhosis.

population: Adults with compensated cirrhosis (no ascites, encephalopathy or variceal bleed) attending hepatology follow-up for at least 12 months. Exclude decompensated patients and those on the transplant list (who have MELD calculated more often for other reasons).
sample: 40 consecutive adults with compensated cirrhosis with at least 2 hepatology reviews in the last 12 months.
data_source: Clinic letters/EPR for MELD documentation; laboratory system for the bilirubin, creatinine and INR used to calculate it.

template.note: Pass criterion: both within 6 months of each other
NICE 1.2.3: indicates high risk of complications

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic MELD calculator to the hepatology clinic letter template that pulls the latest bilirubin, creatinine and INR and flags when the last MELD is more than 6 months old.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same template and sample.
close_loop: Present at hepatology governance; keep the auto-calculator live in the clinic template if it works.
evidence: no audit in the library measures MELD scoring interval adherence in compensated cirrhosis
pitfalls: Bloods done close to, but not attached to, a clinic letter can be missed: search the laboratory system directly, not just letters.
Patients who miss appointments will have gaps that are not the team's fault: record DNA separately from a true miss.
A MELD score without an explicit action plan for a value of 12 or more is a silent gap: capture the 'so what' as well as the number.
Manual MELD calculation is error-prone: check a sample against an online calculator.
pearls: An auto-calculating field in the EPR template removes the main source of missed scores.
Ask biochemistry whether the LIMS can flag a MELD-relevant panel automatically for coded cirrhosis patients.
Use the audit to also check that a rising MELD triggers a specific action (more frequent review, transplant discussion), not just a recorded number.
Keep the definition of 'compensated' consistent between cycles to avoid population drift.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters and lab results
pass: A MELD score is documented in the clinic letter or EPR at least once in each 6-month period for the last 12 months of follow-up.

question: What proportion of adults with cirrhosis and large-volume or refractory ascites who are prescribed a non-selective beta-blocker are prescribed propranolol rather than carvedilol?
why: Carvedilol's added alpha-blocking effect can worsen hypotension and precipitate renal impairment in advanced cirrhosis; no audit in the library checks this medicines-safety point in ascitic patients.

standard.wording: carvedilol should be avoided in people with severe hepatic impairment (for example, in those with large-volume or refractory ascites).

population: Adults with cirrhosis and large-volume or refractory ascites (on the paracentesis list or coded as refractory) currently prescribed a non-selective beta-blocker. Exclude patients on beta-blockers for a cardiac indication only, at a cardiologist's direction.
sample: All patients on the paracentesis/refractory ascites list who are on a beta-blocker (typically 20-40 in a DGH hepatology service over 3-6 months).
data_source: Hepatology paracentesis list and drug chart/e-prescribing for the current beta-blocker and dose.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an e-prescribing alert that fires when carvedilol is prescribed to a patient coded with large-volume or refractory ascites, prompting a switch to propranolol or a documented reason to continue.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same list and sample.
close_loop: Present at hepatology governance and to pharmacy; keep the e-prescribing alert live if it reduces inappropriate carvedilol use.
evidence: no audit in the library checks carvedilol avoidance in cirrhosis with large-volume or refractory ascites
pitfalls: GP-issued prescriptions may lag behind a hospital switch: check the most recent dispensed item, not just the hospital letter.
Some patients are on carvedilol for a genuine cardiac reason agreed with cardiology: exclude these, don't count them as failures.
A single low blood pressure reading is not proof of harm: look for a pattern (hypotension, worsening renal function) alongside the drug choice.
This is a 2023 change: expect resistance from teams used to carvedilol as first-line for variceal prevention generally.
pearls: Run the alert past pharmacy before switching it on, since carvedilol/propranolol substitution needs a dose-equivalent plan, not a straight swap.
Use the hepatology specialist nurse to flag ascites severity accurately, since coding alone under-detects refractory ascites.
Combine data collection with the paracentesis/albumin audit, since it is the same patient list.
Re-check blood pressure and renal function trends at re-audit, not just the drug name, to show the change actually protects patients.
effort: ~15 min per patient from the paracentesis list and drug chart
pass: Patients with large-volume (needing regular paracentesis) or refractory ascites who are on a non-selective beta-blocker are prescribed propranolol, not carvedilol, unless a documented specialist reason is given.

question: What proportion of adults with severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis start enteral nutrition within 72 hours of presentation?
why: Late feeding in severe pancreatitis is linked to worse infective outcomes. The library's pancreatitis topic card shows nutrition is rarely measured at all, with the consultant advice naming it as 'worth doing' [2578, 2680, 2857].

standard.wording: Offer enteral nutrition to anyone with severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis. Start within 72 hours of presentation and aim to meet their nutritional requirements as soon as possible.

population: Adults admitted with acute pancreatitis classified as severe or moderately severe (organ failure, transient or persistent, or local/systemic complications). Exclude mild pancreatitis managed on a normal diet.
sample: 30 consecutive adults with severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis over the last 6-12 months (identify via ITU/HDU admissions and coded pancreatitis with organ support).
data_source: Admission clerking and dietitian notes for severity classification and feeding start time; nursing fluid balance charts for nasogastric feed start.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'nutrition plan by 72 hours' step to the severe pancreatitis care bundle/ITU admission checklist, with an automatic dietitian referral triggered by the severity score.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same bundle and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the upper GI/ITU joint governance meeting; keep the bundle step if enteral feeding starts earlier.
evidence: [2578] a weekly benign upper GI MDT pathway improved imaging and escalation timeliness in pancreatitis but did not report nutrition timing
the library's pancreatitis topic card names nutrition and fluid volumes as rarely measured and worth auditing
pitfalls: Severity classification (moderately severe vs severe) can be applied retrospectively and inconsistently: agree the Atlanta criteria definition with the audit team before starting.
Vomiting or ileus is a valid reason to delay feeding: record it as a reason, not a failure.
ITU and ward notes are often separate systems: check both for the true nutrition start time.
A dietitian referral made is not the same as feed actually starting: capture both timestamps.
pearls: Recruit the ITU dietitian to help identify eligible severe cases and confirm start times.
Agree the Atlanta severity definitions with the audit team in writing before collecting data.
Build the 72-hour target into the same proforma as antibiotic and fluid decisions, since these patients are seen together on ward rounds.
Re-audit after any nutrition team staffing change, since dietitian availability is the main driver of delay.
effort: ~20 min per case from ITU/ward notes and dietitian records
pass: Enteral nutrition (oral, nasogastric or nasojejunal) is started within 72 hours of presentation in patients classified as severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis.

question: What proportion of adults with acute pancreatitis without confirmed or suspected infected pancreatic necrosis are NOT started on prophylactic antibiotics?
why: Routine antibiotics in pancreatitis do not prevent infection and drive resistance, but the library's pancreatitis topic card records inappropriate antibiotic use in 42% and 22 of 56 cases in published audits [2680].

standard.wording: Do not offer prophylactic antimicrobials to people with acute pancreatitis.

population: Adults admitted with a primary diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. Exclude patients with confirmed cholangitis, infected necrosis or another clear infective indication at admission.
sample: 40 consecutive adults admitted with acute pancreatitis over the last 3 months.
data_source: Admission clerking, drug chart/e-prescribing and microbiology requests for antibiotic starts and stated indications.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Remove 'prophylactic antibiotics' as a default order-set item on the acute pancreatitis admission bundle and require a coded indication (necrosis/cholangitis/other infection) before an antibiotic can be prescribed electronically.
reaudit: Repeat in 3 months, same admission bundle.
close_loop: Present at the acute medicine/surgery antimicrobial stewardship meeting; keep the order-set change if inappropriate prescribing falls.
evidence: the library's pancreatitis topic card records inappropriate antibiotic prescribing in 42% of one audit and 22 of 56 patients in another, both without a reported system fix
pitfalls: Distinguishing a genuine early infective complication from reflex prophylaxis needs the clinical picture, not just the drug chart: review the indication written at the time.
Antibiotics started for a co-existing infection (e.g. chest, urine) should not count against the standard: capture the stated reason.
A drop in appropriate use after a locum rotation suggests the order-set change needs repeating at induction.
Retrospective note review can under-detect verbal, unwritten justification: flag unclear cases rather than guessing.
pearls: Get antimicrobial pharmacy involved early; they usually already track inappropriate starts informally.
Make the order-set change the single fix, since the topic card shows teaching alone reached only 65% risk-stratification gains and no reported re-audit for antibiotics specifically.
Feed results back to the acute take induction so new doctors don't reintroduce reflex prescribing.
Track antibiotic duration as well as whether one was started, since stopping a wrongly-started course late is a second failure mode.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the drug chart
pass: No antibiotic is started in the first 48 hours of admission unless there is a documented indication other than prophylaxis (for example, suspected infected necrosis, cholangitis, or a non-pancreatic infection).

question: What proportion of adults who develop necrotic, infective, haemorrhagic or systemic complications of acute pancreatitis have advice sought from a specialist pancreatic centre?
why: Complicated pancreatitis needs specialist input for decisions on drainage, debridement and timing; no audit in the library checks whether this referral step happens.

standard.wording: If a person develops necrotic, infective, haemorrhagic or systemic complications of acute pancreatitis: seek advice from a specialist pancreatic centre within the referral network and discuss whether to move the person to the specialist centre for treatment of the complications.

population: Adults admitted with acute pancreatitis who develop a coded local complication (necrosis, pseudocyst, haemorrhage, abscess) or persistent organ failure. Exclude uncomplicated mild pancreatitis.
sample: All complicated pancreatitis cases identified over 6-12 months in a non-specialist centre (typically 15-30 cases).
data_source: Ward notes, MDT records and referral letters/phone log to the regional specialist pancreatic centre.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'specialist pancreatic centre discussed: yes/date, or why not' field to the ward round proforma whenever a local complication of pancreatitis is coded, with the regional centre's referral hotline number printed on the form.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months given likely small numbers.
close_loop: Present at the upper GI surgery and regional pancreatic network governance meeting; keep the proforma prompt if referral rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks whether specialist pancreatic centre advice is sought for complicated acute pancreatitis
pitfalls: Numbers will be small in most DGHs; a longer collection window or combining a few years' cases may be needed.
Verbal advice given informally (consultant-to-consultant phone call) may not be documented: ask staff to write even brief advice calls in the notes.
Retrospective identification of 'complicated' cases relies on coding accuracy: cross-check with the radiology report for necrosis/collections.
Delayed recognition of the complication itself (not just delayed referral) is a separate problem worth flagging separately.
pearls: Agree the regional referral pathway and contact route with the specialist centre before starting, so 'discussed' has one clear definition.
Use the upper GI MDT as a backstop: any complicated case not yet discussed externally should be flagged there.
Keep a shared log of specialist centre discussions so this audit can be repeated quickly from existing records.
Feed learning back to acute surgical take doctors, who are often the first to see these patients out of hours.
effort: ~20 min per case from ward notes and referral logs
pass: Advice from a specialist pancreatic centre is documented as sought (by phone, MDT or referral letter) within 48 hours of the complication being identified.

question: What proportion of adults with chronic pancreatitis have an HbA1c checked at least every 6 months to monitor for type 3c diabetes?
why: Up to 80% of people with chronic pancreatitis develop diabetes, but there is no audit in the library of whether HbA1c monitoring at the recommended interval actually happens.

standard.wording: Offer people with chronic pancreatitis monitoring of HbA1c for diabetes at least every 6 months.

population: Adults with a coded diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis under specialist or GP shared-care follow-up for at least 12 months. Exclude those already on insulin under a separate diabetes monitoring pathway if that already meets the interval.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with chronic pancreatitis with at least 12 months of follow-up.
data_source: Clinic letters and GP/hospital laboratory system for HbA1c results and dates.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add chronic pancreatitis to the practice/clinic's recall system for 6-monthly HbA1c, with a letter to the GP specifying the interval if follow-up is shared.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months, same sample criteria.
close_loop: Present at the pancreatico-biliary MDT and share with primary care liaison; keep the recall system if adherence improves.
evidence: no audit in the library measures 6-monthly HbA1c monitoring adherence in chronic pancreatitis
pitfalls: Shared care with the GP means results may sit outside the hospital record: check the GP-shared record, not just hospital letters.
New-onset diabetes diagnosed opportunistically should be recorded and cross-checked against the recommended interval going forward.
A recent hospital admission with unrelated bloods can create a false sense that HbA1c is being monitored: check it is specifically HbA1c, not just glucose.
Patients who move between hospital and GP-only follow-up need the recall responsibility made explicit.
pearls: Write the monitoring interval explicitly into the GP discharge/shared-care letter (NICE also expects HbA1c and DEXA frequency communicated to GPs, rec 1.1.7).
Combine this audit's data collection with the bone density audit below, since both come from the same patient list and letters.
A single shared spreadsheet or database recall (hospital or practice-run) is more reliable than depending on individual clinicians remembering.
Re-audit after any change of pancreatico-biliary consultant or specialist nurse, since personal recall systems do not survive rotation.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters and lab results
pass: An HbA1c result is recorded at least once in each 6-month period over the last 12 months of follow-up.

question: What proportion of adults with chronic pancreatitis have a bone density (DEXA) assessment at least every 2 years?
why: Chronic pancreatitis causes malabsorption and steroid-independent bone loss, but there is no audit in the library of DEXA interval adherence in this group.

standard.wording: Offer adults with chronic pancreatitis a bone density assessment every 2 years.

population: Adults with a coded diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis under follow-up for at least 2 years.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with chronic pancreatitis and at least 2 years of follow-up.
data_source: DEXA/imaging reporting system for scan dates; clinic letters for the diagnosis date and follow-up duration.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add chronic pancreatitis patients to a 2-yearly DEXA recall list, requested directly by the pancreatico-biliary team rather than relying on a GP referral.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months, same sample criteria.
close_loop: Present at the pancreatico-biliary MDT; keep the direct-request recall if scan uptake improves.
evidence: no audit in the library measures 2-yearly DEXA interval adherence in chronic pancreatitis
pitfalls: DEXA scans done at another hospital or via a GP osteoporosis pathway can be missed on hospital PACS: ask the patient and check the national image exchange if available.
A DEXA report without a documented follow-up action for osteopenia/osteoporosis is an incomplete pass: capture both.
Waiting-list delays for DEXA are a system issue, not a data error: record the request date as well as the scan date.
Long gaps between clinic reviews can hide overdue scans: check the DEXA system directly rather than only clinic letters.
pearls: A direct hospital-requested DEXA recall avoids the extra step (and drop-off) of asking the GP to refer.
Pair this with the HbA1c audit, since both are follow-up-completeness measures on the same chronic pancreatitis list.
Agree with radiology a standing protocol for chronic pancreatitis DEXA requests so referrals are accepted without individual justification each time.
Feed abnormal results into a bone health pathway (calcium/vitamin D, bisphosphonate referral) so the scan itself changes management.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the DEXA and clinic systems
pass: A DEXA scan report is dated within the last 2 years for the patient's current period of follow-up.

question: What proportion of adults with a positive coeliac serology test are referred to a gastrointestinal specialist for endoscopic biopsy within 6 weeks of the result?
why: Positive serology needs biopsy confirmation before a gluten-free diet starts. The library shows a related process (adequate biopsy sampling) improving from 21.9% to 60.8% after an awareness intervention [6474], but no audit measures referral timeliness after a positive result.

standard.wording: Refer young people and adults with positive serological test results to a gastrointestinal specialist for endoscopic intestinal biopsy to confirm or exclude coeliac disease.

population: Adults (16+) with a positive coeliac serology (tTG or EMA) result in primary or secondary care over the last 6-12 months. Exclude children (paediatric pathway differs) and patients already diagnosed with coeliac disease.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new positive coeliac serology result.
data_source: Laboratory system for the serology result and date; GP/gastroenterology referral system for the referral date; endoscopy system for the biopsy date.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set the laboratory system to auto-generate a gastroenterology 2-week-equivalent referral (or a direct-access endoscopy booking) whenever a positive coeliac serology result is authorised, rather than relying on the requesting clinician to refer.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the gastroenterology and primary care interface meeting; keep the automatic referral trigger if timeliness improves.
evidence: [6474] a duodenal biopsy adequacy audit found only 21.9% of biopsies met the 4-specimen standard, rising to 60.8% after an awareness intervention, showing the coeliac diagnostic pathway needs active management at more than one step
no audit in the library measures time from positive serology to biopsy referral
pitfalls: Patients who have already started a gluten-free diet before referral will have unreliable biopsies: flag and exclude or record separately.
GP referrals sent by letter rather than an electronic pathway are harder to trace: agree one referral route before starting.
A weakly positive result needing EMA confirmation (NICE 1.2.2) adds a step that can be mistaken for delay: record the confirmatory test date too.
Waiting-list pressure on endoscopy is a genuine constraint: separate 'referral made' (clinician-controlled) from 'biopsy done' (partly system-controlled) in the results.
pearls: An automatic referral trigger from the lab removes the main point of failure (a positive result filed without action).
Brief primary care on the 'keep eating gluten until biopsy' message, since this is a common patient safety-netting gap.
Track both referral and biopsy timeliness so any bottleneck (referral vs endoscopy capacity) is clearly identified.
Share results with the endoscopy unit, since a rise in referrals may need a dedicated slot allocation.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the lab and referral systems
pass: A referral for endoscopic biopsy is made within 6 weeks of a positive coeliac serology result, and the patient is advised to continue eating gluten until the biopsy.

question: What proportion of adults with confirmed coeliac disease have a documented annual review that includes weight, symptom review and consideration of dietetic input?
why: Ongoing coeliac care depends on a structured annual review, not just the initial diagnosis; no audit in the library checks whether this review is complete each year.

standard.wording: Offer an annual review to people with coeliac disease. During the review: measure weight and height, review symptoms, consider the need for assessment of diet and adherence to the gluten-free diet, consider the need for specialist dietetic and nutritional advice.

population: Adults with a confirmed diagnosis of coeliac disease under hospital or GP follow-up for at least 12 months.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with confirmed coeliac disease due, or having had, their annual review.
data_source: Gastroenterology or GP annual review clinic letters/EPR template.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build a structured coeliac annual review template (weight, symptoms, dietetic-input decision, vaccination check) into the GP or gastroenterology system, replacing free-text review notes.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months, same template and sample.
close_loop: Present at the gastroenterology-primary care interface meeting; keep the template as the standard annual review record if completeness improves.
evidence: [9569] an invitational letter increased vaccine uptake in coeliac disease from 38.6% to 49.2%, showing structured recall improves an under-performing part of coeliac follow-up
no audit in the library checks completeness of the coeliac annual review itself
pitfalls: Many coeliac annual reviews happen in general practice, sometimes without a distinct template: check GP records, not just hospital letters.
Weight alone without a comparison to a previous value misses faltering weight gain or loss: record trend, not just a single figure.
'Considered' dietetic input can be interpreted loosely: agree what counts as documented consideration before starting (for example, an explicit yes/no with reason).
Patients discharged from hospital follow-up to GP-only care can fall out of any recall system: check both settings for the relevant year.
pearls: A single shared template usable in both primary and secondary care avoids duplicated or missed reviews.
Use the coeliac patient group/dietitian list, if one exists locally, to identify the full eligible population rather than relying on clinic attendance alone.
Bundle the pneumococcal vaccination check into the same template, since NICE links it to coeliac care specifically.
Re-audit after any change to the GP recall system or dietetic staffing, since these reviews often depend on one named clinician.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters or GP records
pass: In the last 12 months, the patient has a review documenting weight, a symptom review, and a decision about dietetic input.

question: What proportion of adults newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have coeliac serology testing at or shortly after diagnosis?
why: Coeliac disease is more common in type 1 diabetes and is easy to miss without proactive testing; no audit in the library checks serology testing rates at diabetes diagnosis.

standard.wording: Offer serological testing for coeliac disease to: people with ... type 1 diabetes, at diagnosis.

population: Adults with a new diagnosis of type 1 diabetes in the last 12-24 months, identified from the diabetes team's new-patient register.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new type 1 diabetes diagnosis.
data_source: Diabetes clinic letters/EPR and laboratory system for coeliac serology requests and results.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add coeliac serology as a pre-selected item on the new type 1 diabetes diagnosis blood panel in the diabetes clinic order set.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months, same register and sample size.
close_loop: Present at the diabetes and gastroenterology joint governance meeting; keep the order-set item if testing rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks coeliac serology testing rates at type 1 diabetes diagnosis
pitfalls: Serology requested by the GP rather than the diabetes team can be missed if only hospital systems are checked.
Symptomatic coeliac disease may have already prompted testing before the diabetes diagnosis: record timing relative to diagnosis, not just whether it was ever done.
A negative result does not exclude future risk: NICE also recommends re-testing if symptoms develop later (rec 1.3.4), which is worth a separate note in results.
New diagnoses made as an inpatient (e.g. with diabetic ketoacidosis) may have this step deprioritised: check both inpatient and outpatient pathways.
pearls: Adding the test to the admission/diagnosis order set is far more reliable than relying on individual clinicians to remember an easily-missed association.
Use the paediatric-to-adult transition list as an additional source of newly diagnosed young adults.
Share results with the diabetes specialist nurses, who often run the new-diagnosis pathway day to day.
Track outcome of positive results through to biopsy referral, not just whether the test was requested.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the diabetes register and lab system
pass: Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA with total IgA) is requested within 3 months of a new type 1 diabetes diagnosis.

question: What proportion of adults started on azathioprine or mercaptopurine for Crohn's disease have thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity checked before the first dose?
why: Starting a thiopurine without checking TPMT risks severe, potentially fatal myelosuppression in deficient patients. A related paediatric audit found TPMT measured in 97% but late (after starting) in 46% of cases [2966], showing timing, not just testing, is the gap.

standard.wording: Assess thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity before offering azathioprine or mercaptopurine. Do not offer azathioprine or mercaptopurine if TPMT activity is deficient (very low or absent). Consider azathioprine or mercaptopurine at a lower dose if TPMT activity is below normal but not deficient.

population: Adults with Crohn's disease newly started on azathioprine or mercaptopurine in the last 12 months. Exclude patients already established on a thiopurine before the audit period.
sample: 30-40 consecutive adults newly started on azathioprine or mercaptopurine for Crohn's disease.
data_source: Gastroenterology clinic letters, e-prescribing and laboratory system for the TPMT request, result and first-dose date.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make TPMT a mandatory, hard-stop pre-requisite field on the electronic thiopurine prescription for IBD, so the first dose cannot be authorised without a documented result.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the gastroenterology and pharmacy governance meeting; keep the hard-stop prescribing rule if pre-dose testing improves.
evidence: [2966] a paediatric gastroenterology azathioprine audit found TPMT measured in 97% of patients but returned late (after starting) in 46%, and shared-care guidelines with order sets were proposed as the fix
no audit in the library measures TPMT-before-first-dose timing in adult Crohn's disease
pitfalls: A TPMT sent on the same day as the first prescription, before the result is back, is a common near-miss: define 'before' as result available, not just sample sent.
Urgent starts (for example, at discharge) are the highest-risk point for skipping the check: flag these specifically.
Local laboratory turnaround time affects feasibility: know the turnaround before setting a hard-stop rule.
GP-initiated repeat prescriptions after a hospital start need the same rule applied, or risk restarting without a recent result after a long gap.
pearls: A pharmacy-enforced hard stop is more reliable than a reminder, since this is a genuine patient-safety risk, not just a documentation gap.
Agree an urgent same-day TPMT turnaround with the laboratory for planned starts, so timeliness does not become an excuse to skip the check.
Audit alongside the ongoing FBC monitoring measure below, since both come from the same thiopurine-start list.
Flag any deficient result found to the whole team immediately, not just recorded, given the severity of the risk it avoids.
effort: ~15 min per patient from e-prescribing and lab results
pass: TPMT activity is checked and the result is available and acted on (standard dose, reduced dose, or drug avoided) before the first dose of azathioprine or mercaptopurine is given.

question: What proportion of adults on ongoing infliximab or adalimumab for Crohn's disease have a documented reassessment of continued need within the last 12 months?
why: Biologics should only continue with evidence of ongoing benefit, but no audit in the library checks whether the 12-monthly reassessment NICE requires is actually done and recorded.

standard.wording: People who continue treatment with infliximab or adalimumab should have their disease reassessed at least every 12 months to determine whether ongoing treatment is still clinically appropriate.

population: Adults with Crohn's disease on infliximab or adalimumab for at least 12 months, identified from the biologics/homecare prescribing list.
sample: 40 consecutive adults on ongoing infliximab or adalimumab for Crohn's disease.
data_source: Gastroenterology clinic letters/EPR and the biologics prescribing or homecare database.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 12-monthly reassessment alert to the biologics prescribing/homecare system that flags any patient approaching 12 months since their last documented review, before the next prescription is authorised.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months, same list and sample.
close_loop: Present at the IBD service governance meeting; keep the prescribing-system alert if reassessment rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library measures 12-monthly reassessment completion for ongoing biologic therapy in Crohn's disease
pitfalls: Biologics given via homecare can be continued on a repeat-prescription basis with limited direct clinical contact: check the homecare database as well as hospital clinic letters.
A telephone or virtual review counts if it is documented with the required content; define this before starting so virtual clinics are not under- or over-counted.
Faecal calprotectin results sitting in a different IT system from the clinic letter can be missed: search the laboratory system directly.
Patients who are stable and rarely seen in person are at highest risk of an undocumented, assumed 'still working' continuation.
pearls: A prescribing-system alert tied to the homecare/biologics pharmacy record catches patients who might otherwise coast without face-to-face review.
Use IBD specialist nurses to run virtual reassessments by phone with a structured symptom and biomarker check, rather than requiring a clinic slot for every patient.
Track the decision made at reassessment (continue/stop/switch), not just whether one happened, to show it changes practice.
Re-audit after any biologics service reconfiguration, since responsibility for review can become unclear during service changes.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the biologics database and clinic letters
pass: A documented reassessment of clinical symptoms, biomarkers (for example, faecal calprotectin or CRP) or investigation is recorded within the last 12 months for each patient continuing infliximab or adalimumab.

question: What proportion of adults admitted with acute severe ulcerative colitis have a documented daily assessment of the likelihood of needing surgery, including stool frequency and CRP?
why: Daily reassessment identifies patients failing medical therapy early enough to escalate safely. The library's topic cards do not include a specific audit of this daily assessment step in acute severe UC.

standard.wording: Assess and document on admission, and then daily, the likelihood of needing surgery for people admitted to hospital with acute severe ulcerative colitis.

population: Adults admitted with acute severe ulcerative colitis (meeting Truelove and Witts' severe criteria). Exclude mild/moderate flares managed as outpatients.
sample: All admissions with acute severe ulcerative colitis over the last 12 months (typically 15-30 cases in a DGH).
data_source: Inpatient ward notes/EPR and laboratory system for daily stool frequency and CRP documentation.

template.note: Pass criterion: recorded on every inpatient day

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a dedicated acute severe UC daily monitoring chart (stool frequency, CRP, pulse, temperature, albumin) kept at the bedside or in the EPR, separate from the general observation chart.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months given likely small numbers.
close_loop: Present at the gastroenterology and colorectal surgery joint IBD meeting; keep the monitoring chart if daily completeness improves.
evidence: no audit in the library measures daily surgical-likelihood assessment completeness in acute severe ulcerative colitis
pitfalls: Weekend and night documentation is the most likely gap: check whether missed days cluster on weekends before proposing a fix.
Retrospective note review can undercount verbal ward-round assessments not written down: only count what is documented, and say so.
Small numbers are expected; consider a rolling collection over 12 months rather than a fixed short window.
A patient transferred to a tertiary centre mid-admission should have their local-stay days counted, not penalised for the transfer.
pearls: A single-page bedside chart used by both medical and nursing staff is easier to complete reliably than relying on free-text ward-round notes.
Involve the IBD clinical nurse specialist, who often already tracks these patients closely.
Pair this with the 72-hour escalation-decision audit below, since both use the same admission cohort and monitoring chart.
Feed missed weekend days back to the acute medical take handover process, not just the gastroenterology team, since cover changes at weekends.
effort: ~20 min per case from ward notes and lab results
pass: Stool frequency and CRP (or another documented surgical-likelihood assessment) are recorded at least once every 24 hours from admission until discharge or surgery.

question: What proportion of adults admitted with acute severe ulcerative colitis who have little or no improvement after 72 hours of intravenous corticosteroids have a documented escalation decision (rescue therapy or surgery) made at that point?
why: Delaying escalation in steroid-refractory acute severe colitis increases the risk of emergency colectomy and complications; no audit in the library measures whether the 72-hour decision point is actually acted on.

standard.wording: Consider adding intravenous ciclosporin to intravenous corticosteroids or consider surgery for people: who have little or no improvement within 72 hours of starting intravenous corticosteroids or whose symptoms worsen at any time despite corticosteroid treatment.

population: Adults admitted with acute severe ulcerative colitis started on IV corticosteroids. Exclude those who clearly improve before 72 hours.
sample: All acute severe UC admissions over 12 months not improving by day 3 (typically 10-20 cases).
data_source: Inpatient ward notes/EPR, including gastroenterology and colorectal surgery joint review entries.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'day 3 acute severe colitis decision' prompt to the joint gastroenterology/colorectal ward round proforma, due exactly 72 hours after IV steroids start.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months given likely small numbers.
close_loop: Present at the gastroenterology and colorectal surgery joint IBD meeting; keep the day-3 prompt if timely escalation improves.
evidence: no audit in the library measures the timeliness of the 72-hour escalation decision in steroid-refractory acute severe ulcerative colitis
pitfalls: The '72 hours' point can fall on a weekend when senior IBD input is less available: check whether delays cluster there.
A verbal decision to 'wait and see' without written reasoning is a common near-miss: require an explicit written plan even if the plan is to continue watching.
Small numbers are expected; combine data over 12 months rather than a short window.
Distinguish patients who improved (correctly not escalated) from those who did not improve but were still not escalated, since only the latter are failures.
pearls: A joint gastroenterology/colorectal ward round on or around day 3 for every acute severe UC admission is the single most effective fix reported for this kind of delay.
Build the 72-hour trigger from the steroid start time recorded in e-prescribing, so the prompt is automatic rather than manually tracked.
Share results with both specialties, since the decision genuinely needs both to be involved (NICE rec 1.2.21).
Track outcomes (colectomy rate, length of stay) at re-audit to show timely escalation is not just paperwork.
effort: ~20 min per case from ward notes
pass: For patients not clearly improving by 72 hours of IV corticosteroids, a documented decision (escalate to ciclosporin/biologic rescue therapy, proceed to surgery, or continue with explicit reasoning) is recorded on day 3 of treatment.

question: What proportion of adults admitted with acute severe ulcerative colitis have a joint gastroenterology and colorectal surgery review documented within 24 hours of admission?
why: NICE requires collaborative gastroenterology-surgical management from the start of an acute severe UC admission; no audit in the library checks whether this joint review happens early enough.

standard.wording: For people admitted to hospital with acute severe ulcerative colitis: ensure that a gastroenterologist and a colorectal surgeon collaborate to provide treatment and management.

population: Adults admitted with acute severe ulcerative colitis (Truelove and Witts' severe criteria).
sample: All acute severe UC admissions over 12 months (typically 15-30 cases).
data_source: Inpatient ward notes/EPR for gastroenterology and colorectal surgery entries and timestamps.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set an automatic referral to colorectal surgery, alongside the gastroenterology referral, whenever 'acute severe colitis' is coded on admission, so both specialties are alerted from the outset rather than surgery being added later.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months given likely small numbers.
close_loop: Present at the joint gastroenterology and colorectal surgery IBD meeting; keep the dual-referral rule if joint input improves.
evidence: no audit in the library measures how quickly colorectal surgery is involved in acute severe ulcerative colitis admissions
pitfalls: Surgical input may be genuinely not needed in every case: only count 'surgery not involved' as a failure if there is no documented reason it was safe to omit.
Out-of-hours admissions may only reach the on-call medical team initially: check whether delays cluster overnight or at weekends.
A surgical opinion recorded as a brief note rather than a full review still counts if it reflects genuine awareness and input: agree the definition in advance.

This audit works best combined with the daily-assessment and 72-hour-escalation audits, since they share the same patient cohort; avoid re-collecting the same admission list three separate times without coordinating.
pearls: A single combined data-collection sheet covering all three acute severe UC audits (this one, daily assessment, and 72-hour escalation) saves duplicate note review.
An automatic dual referral removes reliance on the medical team remembering to involve surgery early.
Use the IBD nurse specialist to flag every acute severe UC admission in real time so both teams are alerted immediately.
Present colectomy rate and length of stay alongside process measures, since joint working is intended to improve these outcomes.
effort: ~15 min per case from ward notes
pass: Both a gastroenterologist and a colorectal surgeon document a review (jointly or separately but within the same 24-hour window) within 24 hours of admission with acute severe ulcerative colitis.

question: What proportion of adults newly diagnosed with MASLD (fatty liver on imaging) have an enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test done to check for advanced fibrosis?
why: Without fibrosis testing, MASLD patients at high risk of progression to cirrhosis are not identified for specialist referral; no audit in the library measures ELF testing uptake in MASLD.

standard.wording: Offer testing for advanced liver fibrosis to people with MASLD. Consider using the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test in people who have been diagnosed with MASLD to test for advanced liver fibrosis.

population: Adults with a new diagnosis of MASLD (steatosis on ultrasound or other imaging plus type 2 diabetes/metabolic syndrome, alcohol excluded) in the last 12 months, identified via radiology reports or GP/hepatology records.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new MASLD diagnosis.
data_source: Radiology reports for the steatosis diagnosis; laboratory system for the ELF request and result; GP/hepatology clinic letters.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic ELF test order (or reflex laboratory pathway) whenever a radiology report codes hepatic steatosis with a coded diagnosis of type 2 diabetes or metabolic syndrome.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the primary care-hepatology interface or metabolic liver disease governance meeting; keep the reflex pathway if testing uptake improves.
evidence: no audit in the library measures ELF testing uptake in newly diagnosed MASLD
pitfalls: MASLD is often diagnosed incidentally on imaging done for another reason (e.g. gallstones): a purely GP-list-based search will miss these cases, so also check radiology reports.
ELF may not be available in every laboratory: confirm local availability and, if using an alternative (e.g. FIB-4), record which test was actually used.
A steatosis report without a documented diagnosis of MASLD in the notes can under-count the true denominator: define inclusion criteria carefully with the audit team.
Following up on an abnormal ELF result (referral to hepatology) is a separate step from testing itself: capture both.
pearls: A reflex laboratory pathway (steatosis + diabetes coded → automatic ELF) avoids relying on individual GPs or hospital clinicians remembering the test.
Engage radiology to standardise wording that flags steatosis clearly in reports, since ambiguous wording is a common cause of missed follow-up.
Use this as an opportunity to build a simple MASLD register, which also supports the HCC/cirrhosis surveillance audits above if advanced fibrosis is confirmed.
Track the proportion referred on for advanced fibrosis, not just tested, to show the pathway works end to end.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from radiology and lab systems
pass: An ELF test (or another advanced fibrosis test used consistently with local pathway) is requested within 6 months of a new MASLD diagnosis being recorded.

question: What proportion of adults diagnosed with advanced liver fibrosis on ELF testing (score ≥10.51) are referred to a hepatology specialist?
why: An abnormal ELF result only helps the patient if it leads to specialist assessment; no audit in the library checks this referral step.

standard.wording: Refer adults and young people diagnosed with advanced liver fibrosis to a relevant specialist in hepatology.

population: Adults with an ELF result of 10.51 or above in the last 12-24 months, identified from the laboratory system.
sample: All patients with an ELF ≥10.51 over the last 12-24 months (likely 15-30 in a typical laboratory catchment).
data_source: Laboratory system for the ELF result; GP/hospital referral system for the hepatology referral date.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set the laboratory system to flag any ELF result ≥10.51 directly to the ordering clinician and to a hepatology virtual clinic inbox, so an abnormal result cannot be filed without a referral decision.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the primary care-hepatology interface meeting; keep the laboratory flagging system if referral rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks referral rates after an abnormal ELF result for advanced fibrosis
pitfalls: A raised ELF result filed in primary care without hospital visibility is the main risk: a shared alert to both GP and a hepatology inbox closes this gap.
Local availability of ELF is limited to some laboratories: numbers may be small, so extend the collection period if needed.
A patient who declines referral should be recorded as such, not as a system failure.
Distinguish a new ELF-based diagnosis of advanced fibrosis from a result in a patient already known to hepatology for another reason.
pearls: A direct laboratory-to-hepatology inbox alert for abnormal ELF results is more reliable than relying on primary care to always act on an unfamiliar test.
Agree a simple 'MASLD-advanced fibrosis' virtual clinic pathway with hepatology so referrals do not need a lengthy standard outpatient wait.
Combine with the ELF-testing audit above as two stages of the same pathway.
Publicise the ELF threshold and referral pathway to GPs, since MASLD referral criteria are still unfamiliar to many.
effort: ~15 min per patient from lab and referral systems
pass: A referral to a hepatology specialist is made within 3 months of an ELF result of 10.51 or above.

question: What proportion of adults started on corticosteroids for severe alcohol-related hepatitis (discriminant function ≥32) have active infection and gastrointestinal bleeding excluded or treated first?
why: Corticosteroids in alcoholic hepatitis increase infection risk if given before sepsis is controlled; no audit in the library checks whether this safety step is followed before starting steroids.

standard.wording: Offer corticosteroid treatment to people with severe alcohol-related hepatitis and a discriminant function of 32 or more, only after: effectively treating any active infection or gastrointestinal bleeding that may be present, controlling any renal impairment, discussing the potential benefits and risks with the person.

population: Adults with severe alcohol-related hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function ≥32) started on corticosteroids in the last 12 months.
sample: All patients started on corticosteroids for severe alcoholic hepatitis over 12 months (typically 10-25 cases).
data_source: Inpatient ward notes/EPR, microbiology results and drug chart for the steroid start date and preceding infection/bleeding assessment.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory pre-steroid checklist (blood cultures, ascitic tap if ascites present, chest X-ray, GI bleeding assessment) to the severe alcoholic hepatitis order set, which must be completed before the steroid prescription can be signed.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months given likely small numbers.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology governance meeting; keep the pre-steroid checklist if compliance improves.
evidence: no audit in the library checks infection or bleeding screening before starting corticosteroids for severe alcoholic hepatitis
pitfalls: Retrospective identification of 'active infection' can be difficult without a systematic screen: define what counts as an adequate screen (cultures, ascitic tap, chest X-ray) before starting.
Numbers are likely to be small: extend the collection period to 12 months or pool across a network.
Steroids sometimes started urgently out of hours before a full screen returns: capture whether the screen was at least sent, even if results were pending.
A documented discussion of risks and benefits with the patient (also required by NICE) is a separate item worth tracking alongside the safety screen.
pearls: Build the checklist into the same order set as the discriminant function calculation, so the safety steps and the treatment decision happen together.
Involve microbiology/infection specialists in agreeing what counts as an adequate pre-steroid screen.
Track 3-month and 1-month mortality alongside process measures, since this is the clinical outcome the safety check protects.
Re-audit after any change in the on-call hepatology or gastroenterology rota, since urgent decisions often fall to whoever is on call.
effort: ~20 min per case from ward notes and results
pass: Before the first dose of corticosteroid, there is documented evidence that infection has been screened for and treated (or excluded) and any GI bleeding has been controlled.

question: What proportion of adults with abnormal liver blood tests and a history of harmful or hazardous drinking are referred to a specialist experienced in alcohol-related liver disease to confirm the diagnosis?
why: A clinical diagnosis of alcohol-related liver disease should be confirmed by a specialist rather than assumed from drinking history alone; no audit in the library checks this referral step. The library shows abnormal LFT follow-up more broadly is under-audited (1 related entry only).

standard.wording: Refer people to a specialist experienced in the management of alcohol-related liver disease to confirm a clinical diagnosis of alcohol-related liver disease.

population: Adults with newly abnormal liver blood tests and a documented history of harmful or hazardous drinking, identified in primary or secondary care over the last 12 months.
sample: 40 consecutive adults meeting these criteria.
data_source: GP/hospital records for the abnormal LFT result, alcohol history and the referral letter/date.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic prompt to the GP or hospital results system: abnormal LFTs plus a coded harmful/hazardous drinking history triggers a suggested hepatology referral rather than a repeat-and-wait approach.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the primary care-hepatology interface meeting; keep the prompt if referral rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks specialist referral rates to confirm a diagnosis of alcohol-related liver disease
pitfalls: Alcohol history documentation is often incomplete, making the denominator hard to define: agree a minimum threshold (for example, an AUDIT-C score or explicit units/week) with the audit team.
Repeat LFTs without referral is a common default: distinguish 'LFTs repeated' from 'referred' clearly in the data.
Other causes of abnormal LFTs (viral hepatitis, drugs, MASLD) need to be genuinely excluded, not assumed, before this pathway applies.
Patients who decline referral or engagement should be recorded as such, not as a service failure.
pearls: A shared primary care-hepatology pathway document, agreed in advance, avoids ambiguity about who refers and when.
Use the alcohol care team or liaison nurse, where one exists, to support engagement with referral for patients who may be ambivalent about it.
Track outcome of the specialist assessment (confirmed ArLD, alternative diagnosis, fibrosis staging) to show the referral changes management.
Re-audit after any change to community alcohol or liver pathway commissioning, since these referral routes can change.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from GP/hospital records
pass: A referral to a hepatology or gastroenterology specialist is made within 3 months of abnormal liver blood tests being identified in a person with harmful or hazardous drinking, once other causes have been excluded.

question: What proportion of adults with pain from chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis are referred to a specialist centre for multidisciplinary assessment?
why: Chronic pancreatitis pain management benefits from specialist multidisciplinary input (pain team, dietetics, endoscopic/surgical options); no audit in the library checks this referral step.

standard.wording: Refer people with pain from chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis to a specialist centre for multidisciplinary assessment.

population: Adults with a diagnosis of chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis and documented ongoing pain, seen in gastroenterology or pain clinic over the last 12 months.
sample: 30 consecutive adults with chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis and pain.
data_source: Gastroenterology/pain clinic letters for the pain assessment and referral to a specialist pancreatic centre.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'persistent pain in chronic pancreatitis: specialist pancreatic centre referral considered' prompt to the gastroenterology clinic template, triggered when pain is coded as ongoing at two consecutive reviews.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months given likely small numbers.
close_loop: Present at the pancreatico-biliary and pain management joint meeting; keep the clinic template prompt if referral rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks referral rates to a specialist pancreatic centre for painful chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis
pitfalls: Pain management is often escalated informally through primary care analgesia rather than referral: capture what was tried locally before assuming referral was appropriate.
Numbers in a single DGH will be small: extend the collection period or combine with neighbouring units.
Ongoing alcohol use complicates referral acceptance and outcome: record engagement with alcohol support as context, not as a reason to withhold referral.
A referral made but not yet seen (long waiting list) should be recorded as 'referred', with the wait time as a separate issue to escalate.
pearls: Agree the regional specialist pancreatic centre referral route and typical waiting time before starting, so expectations are realistic.
Loop in the chronic pain team locally as a bridge while a specialist centre referral is pending.
Track whether alcohol support was also offered alongside pain referral, since ongoing drinking undermines both problems.
Use this audit to also flag whether surgical options (see NICE NG104 on duct obstruction) were considered at the specialist assessment.
effort: ~15 min per case from clinic letters
pass: A referral to a specialist pancreatic centre for multidisciplinary assessment is made and documented for patients with ongoing pain from chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis not controlled by simple analgesia.

question: What proportion of adults treated for delirium tremens in hospital are prescribed oral lorazepam as first-line treatment before parenteral treatment?
why: First-line drug choice for delirium tremens affects both safety and the ability to reassess response; the library's alcohol withdrawal topic card shows scoring and specialist oversight are weak points, but does not track first-line drug choice for delirium tremens specifically.

standard.wording: In people with delirium tremens, offer oral lorazepam as first-line treatment. If symptoms persist or oral medication is declined, offer parenteral lorazepam or haloperidol.

population: Adults diagnosed with delirium tremens during an inpatient admission for alcohol withdrawal in the last 6-12 months.
sample: 30 consecutive adults with a documented diagnosis of delirium tremens.
data_source: Inpatient ward notes/EPR and drug chart for the sequence of drugs given.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add delirium tremens as a specific pathway on the alcohol withdrawal order set, with oral lorazepam pre-selected as the default first step and parenteral options only unlocked after a documented reason.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the alcohol care/liaison psychiatry governance meeting; keep the order-set default if first-line prescribing improves.
evidence: the library's alcohol withdrawal topic card shows addiction specialist oversight on acute wards was as low as 4%, suggesting structured prescribing pathways are needed rather than relying on individual clinical judgement for complications like delirium tremens
pitfalls: Patients too agitated to safely take oral medication are a genuine reason to start parenteral treatment first: record this as a valid reason, not a failure.
Out-of-hours decisions may default to whatever is easiest to draw up (often parenteral): check whether time of day predicts drug choice.

A general alcohol withdrawal order set without a specific delirium tremens pathway can blur the distinction between routine and DT management: confirm the diagnosis is explicit before including a case.
Reviewing the withdrawal regimen after DT develops (1.1.4.2) is a second, separate standard worth capturing alongside first-line drug choice.
pearls: A default order-set option removes the need for staff to recall the correct sequence under pressure.
Loop in liaison psychiatry or an alcohol care team, if one exists, since delirium tremens often triggers a specialist review anyway.
Use ward pharmacy to spot-check compliance in real time, not just retrospectively.
Track whether the withdrawal regimen is actively reviewed after DT develops, since this is often forgotten once acute treatment is given.
effort: ~15 min per case from ward notes and drug chart
pass: Oral lorazepam is tried first, with parenteral treatment reserved for persistent symptoms or where oral medication is declined or not possible.

question: What proportion of adults treated for suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy receive parenteral thiamine for a minimum of 5 days before switching to oral thiamine?
why: Stopping parenteral thiamine too early risks permanent Korsakoff's psychosis. The library's alcohol topic card shows Pabrinex timing is measured, but not treatment duration once started; no audit checks the 5-day minimum specifically.

standard.wording: Offer parenteral thiamine to people with suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy ... Parenteral treatment should be given for a minimum of 5 days, unless Wernicke's encephalopathy is excluded. Oral thiamine treatment should follow parenteral therapy.

population: Adults treated for suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy (any one or more of the classic triad, or high clinical risk with prophylactic-dose escalation to treatment dose) in the last 6-12 months.
sample: 30 consecutive adults treated for suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy.
data_source: Inpatient ward notes/EPR and drug chart for the parenteral thiamine start and stop dates and the switch to oral thiamine.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 5-day course length to the parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) prescription for suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy in e-prescribing, requiring a documented reason to stop earlier.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the alcohol care/hepatology governance meeting; keep the 5-day prescribing default if course completion improves.
evidence: no audit in the library checks whether parenteral thiamine for suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy is continued for the recommended minimum 5 days
pitfalls: Early discharge is a common reason parenteral thiamine is stopped prematurely: a discharge plan should include continuing IM thiamine or an alternative if inpatient days fall short of 5.
'Suspected' Wernicke's is subjective: agree a working definition (any one of the triad, or high risk plus a clinical decision to treat) with the audit team.
Drug chart gaps (missed doses) should be distinguished from a deliberate early stop.
A switch straight to oral thiamine without any parenteral treatment at all is a different, more serious failure than stopping parenteral treatment slightly early: capture both separately.
pearls: Build a 5-day default course into the e-prescribing order, since manual daily re-prescribing is the main point where doses get missed or stopped early.
Arrange IM thiamine continuation in the community or via an alcohol liaison team for patients who could otherwise be discharged before day 5.
Use this audit's data collection to also spot-check that the correct high dose (BNF upper range) is used, not just that thiamine was given.
Share results with the emergency department and acute medical take, since under-treatment often starts at first presentation, not on the specialist ward.
effort: ~15 min per case from the drug chart
pass: Parenteral thiamine (for example, IV/IM Pabrinex) is continued for at least 5 days, or is stopped earlier only with a documented reason that Wernicke's encephalopathy has been excluded, followed by oral thiamine.

question: What proportion of adults with acute upper GI bleeding have a full Rockall score documented after endoscopy?
why: A published local audit found the related pre-endoscopy Blatchford score was used in only 12.5% of cases, improving to 50% after teaching [2283]; a second audit found post-OGD full Rockall scoring only improved after an electronic action set was introduced [5670]. No audit in the library measures full post-endoscopy Rockall documentation as its own standard.

standard.wording: Use the following formal risk assessment scores for all patients with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding: the Blatchford score at first assessment, and the full Rockall score after endoscopy.

population: Adults admitted with acute upper GI bleeding who have an endoscopy during the admission. Exclude patients who die or are too unstable for endoscopy.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with acute upper GI bleeding who had an endoscopy over the last 3 months.
data_source: Endoscopy report and ward notes/EPR for the documented Rockall score.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory full Rockall score field to the endoscopy reporting system template for all upper GI bleed procedures, calculated from pre-filled clinical and endoscopic findings.
reaudit: Repeat in 3 months, same sample size.
close_loop: Present at the endoscopy unit and acute medicine governance meeting; keep the mandatory template field if documentation improves.
evidence: [2283] a district general hospital audit of upper GI bleeding found low use of formal risk scores at baseline, improving only partially after teaching alone
[5670] an electronic 'action set' significantly improved post-OGD full Rockall documentation compared with teaching and guidelines alone
pitfalls: A pre-endoscopy (admission) Rockall score is sometimes recorded instead of the full post-endoscopy score: check the field explicitly includes endoscopic findings.
Patients who have emergency surgery instead of endoscopy should be excluded, not counted as missing data.
