Teaching-only interventions have repeatedly shown only partial, non-durable gains in this exact measure [2283]; plan for an electronic or template fix from the outset rather than teaching alone.
Endoscopists working across multiple sites may use different reporting systems: confirm the field is mandatory in all systems used locally.
pearls: An electronic action set embedded in the endoscopy reporting system has already been shown to work for this exact measure [5670]; replicate that approach rather than starting from teaching.
Auto-calculate the score from fields already entered (age, comorbidity, shock, diagnosis, stigmata) so completion does not add extra work.
Use the score to also verify safe early discharge of low-risk patients, not just as a box-ticking exercise.
Re-audit promptly after the template change, since electronic fixes in this specific measure have shown fast, large gains.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from the endoscopy system
pass: A full (post-endoscopy) Rockall score, including endoscopic findings, is calculated and documented in the notes or endoscopy report after the index endoscopy.

question: What proportion of adults admitted with upper GI bleeding who are taking a regular NSAID (excluding low-dose aspirin) have it stopped during the acute admission?
why: Continuing NSAIDs during active or recent GI bleeding increases rebleeding risk; no audit in the library checks NSAID discontinuation specifically, as opposed to aspirin continuation.

standard.wording: Stop other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (including cyclooxygenase-2 [COX-2] inhibitors) during the acute phase in patients presenting with upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

population: Adults admitted with upper GI bleeding who were taking a regular NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor before admission. Exclude low-dose aspirin taken for secondary cardiovascular prevention.
sample: 30 consecutive adults with upper GI bleeding on a regular NSAID at admission, over the last 6 months.
data_source: Admission drug history, drug chart/e-prescribing and discharge summary.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic e-prescribing alert that flags any regular NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor on the drug chart of a patient coded with upper GI bleeding, prompting the prescriber to stop it or document a reason to continue.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the acute medicine and pharmacy governance meeting; keep the e-prescribing alert if discontinuation rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks NSAID discontinuation rates in acute upper GI bleeding, as distinct from aspirin management
pitfalls: NSAIDs prescribed by a GP but not listed clearly on the hospital drug chart can be missed: check the admission medicines reconciliation carefully.
Distinguishing regular NSAID use from occasional over-the-counter use needs a clear history, which is not always well documented.
The discharge summary is the last safety-net point: a drug stopped on the ward but restarted by default on discharge (because it was on a repeat list) is still a failure.
Alternative analgesia not being offered can drive patients to restart NSAIDs themselves after discharge: consider tracking this too.
pearls: An e-prescribing alert linked to the GI bleed diagnosis code is more reliable than expecting every prescriber to remember on a busy take.
Make sure the discharge summary explicitly states the NSAID was stopped and why, so GPs do not restart it on a routine medication review.
Offer a paracetamol/weak-opioid alternative pathway alongside stopping the NSAID, to reduce the temptation to restart it for pain.
Distinguish and separately report low-dose aspirin (which NICE says to continue) so the two messages are not confused by staff.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the drug chart
pass: Any regular NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor (other than low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention) is stopped by the time of discharge from the acute admission.

question: What proportion of adults who rebleed after initial endoscopic treatment for upper GI bleeding have a repeat endoscopy offered, with a view to further treatment or surgery?
why: Rebleeding after endoscopic haemostasis is a recognised high-risk event; no audit in the library checks whether repeat endoscopy is offered as recommended when it happens.

standard.wording: Offer a repeat endoscopy to patients who re-bleed with a view to further endoscopic treatment or emergency surgery.

population: Adults who had endoscopic treatment for non-variceal upper GI bleeding and then had a clinically confirmed rebleed during the same admission, over the last 12 months.
sample: All confirmed rebleeds after endoscopic treatment over 12 months (typically 10-20 cases in a DGH).
data_source: Ward notes/EPR and endoscopy reporting system for the rebleed event, subsequent endoscopy, and any surgical or interventional radiology referral.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'confirmed rebleed' escalation pathway to the GI bleed proforma that automatically prompts an urgent repeat endoscopy request (or direct surgical/interventional radiology referral if endoscopy is not appropriate) rather than a routine re-referral.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months given likely small numbers.
close_loop: Present at the upper GI bleed governance meeting (gastroenterology, surgery, interventional radiology); keep the escalation pathway if timely repeat treatment improves.
evidence: no audit in the library checks whether repeat endoscopy is offered to patients who rebleed after initial endoscopic treatment
pitfalls: Numbers are likely to be small in a single centre; extend the collection period to 12 months.
Rebleeding can be missed or delayed in recognition if nursing observations are not escalated promptly: consider auditing recognition time as well as treatment time.
Out-of-hours rebleeds may default to surgical referral without repeat endoscopy being considered first, which may be appropriate but should be a documented decision, not a default.
Distinguish a genuine rebleed from ongoing slow bleeding not yet controlled, which follows a different initial pathway.
pearls: Agree a clear definition of 'rebleed' (for example, further melaena/haematemesis with a haemodynamic change) with the audit team before starting.
A single-page escalation pathway readily available on the acute take and gastroenterology on-call phone line helps out-of-hours decision-making.
Track the interval from rebleed recognition to repeat procedure, not just whether one happened, since speed matters clinically.
Share results with interventional radiology, since they are part of the same escalation pathway for unstable rebleeds.
effort: ~20 min per case from ward notes and endoscopy reports
pass: A repeat endoscopy is offered (and performed, or a documented reason given for proceeding straight to surgery or interventional radiology) for patients who rebleed after initial endoscopic treatment.

question: What proportion of adults given terlipressin for suspected variceal bleeding have it stopped once definitive haemostasis is achieved, or by 5 days, whichever is sooner?
why: Terlipressin causes ischaemic complications and should not be continued longer than needed; no audit in the library checks course duration, as distinct from whether it was started before endoscopy.

standard.wording: Offer terlipressin to patients with suspected variceal bleeding at presentation. Stop treatment after definitive haemostasis has been achieved, or after 5 days, unless there is another indication for its use.

population: Adults started on terlipressin for suspected or confirmed variceal bleeding in the last 6-12 months.
sample: 30 consecutive adults started on terlipressin for suspected variceal bleeding.
data_source: Drug chart/e-prescribing for start and stop dates; endoscopy report for confirmation of haemostasis.

template.note: Pass criterion: at haemostasis or by day 5

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic 5-day maximum duration and a 'stop if haemostasis confirmed' prompt to the terlipressin prescription in e-prescribing, requiring a documented reason to continue beyond either trigger.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology and pharmacy governance meeting; keep the e-prescribing duration limit if appropriate stopping improves.
evidence: no audit in the library checks terlipressin course duration or stopping practice after variceal bleeding
pitfalls: Terlipressin sometimes continues by default on a drug chart after endoscopy has confirmed haemostasis, simply because no one actively stops it: this is the main failure mode to look for.
A small number of patients need terlipressin continued for hepatorenal syndrome, a valid separate indication: exclude or flag these clearly.
Weekend handovers are a common point where a 'stop by day 5' plan is lost: check whether stop delays cluster around weekends.
Ischaemic side effects (digital, cardiac, mesenteric) are a rare but serious outcome worth recording if found, even though numbers will be small.
pearls: An e-prescribing hard stop at day 5 is a simple, durable fix that does not depend on staff remembering.
Make the endoscopy report a trigger: a 'terlipressin can stop now' flag when haemostasis is confirmed, linked to the drug chart.
Brief nursing and junior medical staff that terlipressin is not a default 3-5 day course regardless of endoscopy findings.
Track ischaemic adverse events over time as a secondary outcome measure, even if numbers are too small for statistics.
effort: ~15 min per case from the drug chart
pass: Terlipressin is stopped once definitive haemostasis is documented at endoscopy, or by day 5 at the latest, unless another indication (for example, hepatorenal syndrome) is documented.

question: What proportion of adults started on acid-suppression therapy for stress ulcer prophylaxis in critical care have its ongoing need reviewed when they recover or are discharged from critical care?
why: Acid-suppression started for critical illness is commonly continued unreviewed on the ward and after hospital discharge; no audit in the library checks this specific review step.

standard.wording: Review the ongoing need for acid-suppression drugs for primary prevention of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in acutely ill patients when they recover or are discharged from critical care.

population: Adults started on a PPI or H2-receptor antagonist for stress ulcer prophylaxis (not for another indication such as known peptic ulcer disease) during a critical care admission in the last 3 months.
sample: 40 consecutive adults started on acid-suppression prophylaxis in critical care.
data_source: Critical care and ward drug charts/e-prescribing, and the critical care outreach or discharge summary.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'stress ulcer prophylaxis: stop or continue with reason' field to the critical care discharge/step-down checklist, so the decision is made before the patient leaves the unit.
reaudit: Repeat in 3 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the critical care and pharmacy governance meeting; keep the discharge checklist field if review rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks review of stress ulcer prophylaxis at critical care discharge
pitfalls: Acid-suppression started for a genuine indication (known peptic ulcer disease, reflux) should be excluded from the denominator, since ongoing treatment is then appropriate rather than a review failure.

Ward teams receiving the patient after critical care discharge may not know the drug was started as prophylaxis rather than for an established indication: make the reason for starting visible on the drug chart from the outset.
The drug can continue unreviewed all the way to hospital discharge and onto a GP repeat prescription: track this endpoint too, not just critical care discharge.
A documented review that concludes 'continue' without a stated reason is a partial pass at best: require an explicit reason.
pearls: A structured critical care discharge checklist is the natural place for this review, since it already covers other medicines reconciliation items.
Label the indication ('stress ulcer prophylaxis') clearly on the drug chart at the time of starting, so it is not mistaken for a standing indication later.
Loop in ward pharmacists to review stress ulcer prophylaxis specifically on step-down wards, as a safety net if the critical care checklist is missed.
Track whether the drug is still being taken at hospital discharge and, ideally, at a GP medication review, to close the loop fully.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from drug charts and discharge summaries
pass: A documented decision to continue or stop acid-suppression prophylaxis is made at the point of critical care discharge (or recovery from the acute illness if remaining on the unit).

question: What proportion of adults aged 40 and over presenting with jaundice are referred using a suspected cancer pathway referral for pancreatic cancer within 2 working days?
why: Delayed recognition of jaundice as a possible pancreatic cancer symptom delays diagnosis and treatment. A related audit of delays in managing suspected pancreatic malignancy found a median of 9 days from presentation to referral for specialist MDT discussion [2287], showing this step is not yet reliably timely.

standard.wording: Refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for pancreatic cancer if they are aged 40 and over and have jaundice.

population: Adults aged 40 and over presenting to primary care, the emergency department or an acute medical take with new jaundice, over the last 6-12 months. Exclude patients with a known, already-investigated benign cause (for example, known gallstones on prior imaging).
sample: 30-40 consecutive adults aged 40+ presenting with new jaundice.
data_source: GP/ED/acute medicine records for the jaundice presentation and the 2-week-wait referral system for the referral date.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add jaundice in a patient aged 40+ as a hard-coded trigger on the GP and ED referral systems that pre-populates a suspected cancer pathway referral for pancreatic (and biliary) cancer, rather than relying on the clinician to remember the age/symptom combination.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the primary care-cancer services interface meeting and the upper GI cancer MDT; keep the referral trigger if timeliness improves.
evidence: [2287] an audit of delays in managing suspected pancreatic malignancy found a median 9-day delay from presentation to MDT referral, with no reported system fix to close this specific gap
pitfalls: Jaundice identified incidentally on blood tests (rather than clinically obvious) can be missed if only clinical documentation is searched: also check bilirubin results directly.

A clear, recently confirmed benign cause (known gallstone disease already under active management) should be excluded from the denominator, but this exclusion needs to be genuinely documented, not assumed.
ED presentations out of hours may default to 'admit and investigate' without an explicit 2-week-wait referral being made in parallel: check both routes.
Referral timeliness is only useful if the pathway itself is fast: also track time from referral to first MDT discussion, as the related audit found this step is also delayed [2287].
pearls: A hard-coded age-plus-symptom prompt in the referral system removes reliance on individual clinicians recalling the NICE criterion.
Agree with radiology/hepatobiliary surgery a fast-track imaging slot for suspected pancreatic cancer referrals, since imaging is usually the next rate-limiting step.
Present results to both primary care and the acute take, since jaundice can present in either setting.
Track the full pathway (presentation to referral to first MDT discussion to treatment) over time, since referral speed alone will not fix downstream delays shown in [2287].
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from referral and results systems
pass: A suspected cancer pathway (2-week-wait) referral for pancreatic cancer is made within 2 working days of jaundice being identified in a patient aged 40 or over, unless an alternative, clearly benign cause is already established.

question: What proportion of adults with cirrhosis given prophylactic intravenous antibiotics for upper GI bleeding have the antibiotic reviewed (continued, switched or stopped) by 72 hours?
why: Prophylactic antibiotics for GI bleeding in cirrhosis are often started appropriately but then continued by default; the existing library and proposed audits cover starting antibiotics before endoscopy, but no audit checks the review step once started.

standard.wording: Review the use of intravenous antibiotics prescribed for upper gastrointestinal bleeding in line with the section on prescribing intravenous antimicrobials in NICE's guideline on antimicrobial stewardship.

population: Adults with cirrhosis started on IV antibiotics for upper GI bleeding in the last 6 months.
sample: 30 consecutive adults with cirrhosis started on IV antibiotics for GI bleeding.
data_source: Drug chart/e-prescribing and microbiology ward round notes.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 72-hour IV antibiotic review alert (forcing a continue/switch/stop decision) to the e-prescribing system for any antibiotic started under a GI bleed indication code.
reaudit: Repeat in 6 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the antimicrobial stewardship and hepatology joint meeting; keep the 72-hour alert if review rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks the 72-hour antibiotic review step for GI bleeding in cirrhosis, as distinct from whether antibiotics were started at all
pitfalls: An antibiotic continued because the patient develops a new, separate infection should be recorded as an appropriate continuation, not a stewardship failure.
Weekend cover can cause reviews to slip past 72 hours: check whether delays cluster there.
Distinguish antibiotics started specifically for GI bleed prophylaxis from those started for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or another confirmed infection, which follow different courses.
Retrospective note review can miss brief verbal ward-round decisions: only count what is documented, and note this limitation.
pearls: A 72-hour hard-stop-style alert is consistent with the same principle already used successfully for surgical prophylaxis elsewhere; adapt that model.
Involve the antimicrobial pharmacist to review these patients proactively rather than relying on the medical team alone.
Pair data collection with the existing IV-antibiotics-before-endoscopy measure, since both use the same patient list.
Track total antibiotic duration as an outcome measure alongside whether a review happened.
effort: ~15 min per case from the drug chart
pass: A documented antimicrobial review (continue, switch to oral, or stop) is recorded within 72 hours of starting IV antibiotics for GI bleeding in a patient with cirrhosis.

question: What proportion of adults with refractory ascites due to cirrhosis have a documented assessment for a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)?
why: Refractory ascites carries a poor prognosis without TIPS or transplant assessment; no audit in the library checks whether TIPS is actively considered in this group, beyond related audits of paracentesis technique.

standard.wording: Consider a TIPS procedure for people with cirrhosis who have refractory ascites.

population: Adults with cirrhosis coded as having refractory ascites (needing large-volume paracentesis at least every 2 weeks, or diuretic-unresponsive/intolerant ascites) in the last 12 months.
sample: All patients meeting refractory ascites criteria over 12 months (typically 15-30 in a DGH hepatology service).
data_source: Hepatology clinic letters/EPR and the paracentesis list for frequency of large-volume paracentesis.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add refractory ascites (based on paracentesis frequency) as an automatic flag on the hepatology paracentesis list that prompts a TIPS/transplant suitability discussion at the next MDT.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology MDT and interventional radiology joint meeting; keep the automatic flag if assessment rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks TIPS assessment rates in refractory ascites, as distinct from paracentesis technique itself
pitfalls: Some patients are clearly unsuitable for TIPS (severe encephalopathy, advanced heart failure) and this should count as meeting the standard if documented, not as a missed opportunity.
Refractory ascites definitions vary; agree a clear, paracentesis-frequency-based definition with the audit team before starting.
Patients already listed for or having had a liver transplant assessment may reasonably have TIPS deprioritised: capture this context.
Retrospective identification from the paracentesis list may miss patients managed with fewer, larger-volume taps: cross-check with clinic letters too.
pearls: Use the paracentesis list itself as the simplest way to identify the eligible population, since these patients are already being tracked for another reason.
Build the TIPS/transplant discussion into an existing regular MDT rather than creating a new meeting.
Loop in interventional radiology early, since they will need to give a technical suitability opinion alongside the hepatology assessment.
Track outcomes (TIPS performed, transplant listed, or neither with reason) at re-audit to show the assessment step leads to a real decision.
effort: ~15 min per patient from the paracentesis list and clinic letters
pass: A documented decision about TIPS suitability (referred for assessment, or a specific reason why not suitable, for example advanced encephalopathy or severe liver failure) is recorded for patients meeting criteria for refractory ascites.

question: What proportion of adults drinking above the high-risk threshold (men >50, women >35 units/week for several months) have transient elastography offered to check for cirrhosis?
why: Early detection of cirrhosis in heavy drinkers allows earlier intervention, but no audit in the library checks whether transient elastography is offered at the recommended drinking threshold, as distinct from general alcohol screening.

standard.wording: Offer transient elastography to diagnose cirrhosis for: ... men and people registered male at birth who drink over 50 units of alcohol per week and have done so for several months; women and people registered female at birth who drink over 35 units of alcohol per week and have done so for several months; people diagnosed with alcohol-related liver disease.

population: Adults with a documented alcohol history meeting the NICE high-risk threshold (men >50, women >35 units/week for several months), identified from alcohol liaison, GP or gastroenterology records over the last 12 months.
sample: 40 consecutive adults meeting the high-risk drinking threshold.
data_source: Alcohol liaison/GP/gastroenterology records for the drinking history; radiology/hepatology system for the transient elastography referral and result.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic transient elastography referral prompt to the alcohol liaison and GP alcohol-history template whenever units/week above the NICE threshold are recorded.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the alcohol care team and hepatology interface meeting; keep the referral prompt if uptake improves.
evidence: no audit in the library checks transient elastography offer rates at the specific high-risk drinking threshold defined by NICE
pitfalls: A full, quantified drinking history (units/week and duration) is often missing from records, making the denominator hard to define: agree a minimum documentation standard before starting.
Some services already scan all heavy drinkers routinely and this may look like a ceiling effect: check local pathway assumptions before assuming a gap exists.
Elastography referred but not attended should be recorded separately from not offered, since these need different fixes (engagement support versus system prompts).
Patients already known to have cirrhosis do not need this specific test again: exclude them from the denominator.
pearls: Use the alcohol care team, where one exists, as the most reliable route to both take a full drinking history and refer for elastography in one contact.
A community-based (rather than hospital-only) scanning service increases uptake for patients reluctant to attend hospital appointments.
Track attendance as well as referral, since engagement is often the bigger barrier in this population.
Feed positive findings into the wider cirrhosis surveillance pathway audited elsewhere in this set.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from alcohol liaison and hepatology records
pass: Transient elastography is offered (referral made, whether or not the patient attends) within 3 months of a documented drinking history meeting the high-risk threshold.

question: What proportion of adults with alcohol-related liver disease, or MASLD with advanced fibrosis, who do not have cirrhosis are retested for cirrhosis at least every 2 years?
why: People at ongoing risk of progressing to cirrhosis need periodic retesting, not a one-off negative result; no audit in the library checks this retesting interval.

standard.wording: Offer retesting for cirrhosis every 2 years for: people diagnosed with alcohol-related liver disease, people with hepatitis C virus infection who have not shown a sustained virological response to antiviral therapy, people with MASLD and advanced liver fibrosis.

population: Adults with alcohol-related liver disease or MASLD with advanced fibrosis, previously tested for cirrhosis and found not to have it, under follow-up for at least 2 years.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible adults with at least 2 years since their last negative cirrhosis test.
data_source: Hepatology/gastroenterology clinic letters and the elastography/imaging system for test dates.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 2-yearly recall for cirrhosis retesting to the hepatology or GP chronic liver disease register for eligible patients, rather than relying on ad hoc re-referral.
reaudit: Repeat in 12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology governance meeting; keep the recall register if retesting adherence improves.
evidence: no audit in the library measures 2-yearly cirrhosis retesting adherence in patients at ongoing risk
pitfalls: Patients who stop attending follow-up (including due to ongoing alcohol use) are the group most likely to miss retesting, and also the group at highest risk: flag non-attendance rather than silently excluding these patients.
A retest done for another reason (e.g. incidental imaging) may satisfy the standard even if not labelled as a 'retest': check imaging history broadly, not just labelled follow-up scans.
Local availability of transient elastography devices limits capacity: record whether delay reflects service capacity rather than a process failure.
Patients who progress to cirrhosis between scheduled retests should be picked up by symptoms/blood tests, not solely by the fixed interval: note any such cases separately.
pearls: A chronic liver disease register with an automatic recall function is the most reliable fix; building this once benefits several of the audits in this set.
Community alcohol and liver clinics can help retain patients who might otherwise disengage from hospital follow-up.
Use this audit as an opportunity to build or refine a shared hepatology-primary care register, since retesting often depends on GP-hospital communication.
Report retesting adherence separately by diagnosis group (ArLD vs MASLD vs HCV), since engagement patterns often differ.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters and imaging records
pass: A repeat test for cirrhosis (transient elastography or equivalent) is documented within 2 years of the previous negative test in eligible patients.

question: What proportion of adults with decompensated alcohol-related liver disease, still decompensated after best management and 3 months' abstinence, are referred for assessment for liver transplantation?
why: Liver transplant referral criteria for alcohol-related liver disease are specific and time-defined; no audit in the library checks whether eligible patients are actually referred once they meet them.

standard.wording: Refer patients with decompensated liver disease to be considered for assessment for liver transplantation if they: still have decompensated liver disease after best management and 3 months' abstinence from alcohol and are otherwise suitable candidates for liver transplantation.

population: Adults with alcohol-related decompensated liver disease under hepatology follow-up, documented as abstinent for 3 months or more, and still decompensated, over the last 12-24 months.
sample: All patients meeting these criteria over 12-24 months (typically 10-20 cases in a DGH hepatology service).
data_source: Hepatology clinic letters/EPR for decompensation status, abstinence duration, and the transplant centre referral letter.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a '3-month abstinence and still decompensated: transplant referral considered' prompt to the hepatology follow-up template, triggered automatically once 3 months of documented abstinence is reached in a decompensated patient.
reaudit: Repeat in 12-24 months given likely small numbers.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology MDT and regional transplant network meeting; keep the follow-up template prompt if referral rates improve.
evidence: no audit in the library checks referral rates for liver transplant assessment against the specific NICE 3-month abstinence criterion
pitfalls: Confirming '3 months' abstinence' reliably (self-report versus biochemical markers) is itself inconsistent between clinicians: agree a documentation standard before starting.
Some patients are correctly not referred due to other contraindications (severe cardiac or psychiatric comorbidity): capture these as valid reasons, not failures.
Numbers will be small; extend the collection period or audit retrospectively over 24 months.
A patient who relapses during the 3-month period restarts the clock under most local pathways: record this clearly rather than treating it as an audit exclusion only.
pearls: A structured alcohol-abstinence tracking field (rather than free text) makes this measurable and repeatable.
Engage the regional transplant centre early to confirm the exact local interpretation of 'suitable candidate' criteria used alongside the NICE recommendation.
Loop in the alcohol liaison or addiction service, since abstinence support is central to whether patients ever reach the 3-month point at all.
Present outcomes of transplant centre assessments (accepted, declined, further tests needed) to close the loop beyond referral alone.
effort: ~20 min per patient from clinic letters
pass: A referral to a liver transplant centre for assessment is made and documented for patients who remain decompensated after best medical management and 3 months' confirmed abstinence, and who have no other clear contraindication.

question: What proportion of adults on azathioprine or mercaptopurine for Crohn's disease have a full blood count checked at the locally agreed monitoring interval, even when TPMT activity is normal?
why: Neutropenia can occur on thiopurines despite normal TPMT activity, so ongoing monitoring remains essential; a related paediatric audit found only 24.5% of patients were fully compliant with blood monitoring frequency [2966]. No audit in the library measures this in adult IBD.

standard.wording: Monitor the effects of azathioprine, mercaptopurine and methotrexate as advised in the BNF or BNFC. Consult the monographs of individual drugs for advice on monitoring immunosuppressives. Monitor for neutropenia in people taking azathioprine or mercaptopurine even if they have normal TPMT activity.

population: Adults on ongoing azathioprine or mercaptopurine for Crohn's disease for at least 6 months, identified from the biologics/immunosuppressant prescribing list.
sample: 40 consecutive adults on ongoing azathioprine or mercaptopurine.
data_source: Laboratory system for FBC dates and results; shared-care monitoring record if monitoring is done in primary care.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Set up a shared-care monitoring template (hospital or GP-run) with an automatic reminder when an FBC becomes overdue for any patient on ongoing thiopurine therapy for IBD.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same list and sample.
close_loop: Present at the IBD and shared-care governance meeting; keep the reminder system if compliance improves.
evidence: [2966] a paediatric azathioprine monitoring audit found only 24.5% of patients fully compliant with the recommended blood monitoring frequency, and proposed a shared-care guideline with a tick-box proforma as the fix
pitfalls: Shared-care monitoring split between GP and hospital can create gaps where each assumes the other is checking: agree and document one named responsible party per patient.
Missed appointments for blood tests are common and should be flagged for active follow-up, not just recorded as a gap.
A late-but-eventually-done blood test still represents a period of unmonitored risk: report both 'ever done' and 'done on time'.
Dose changes reset or alter the expected monitoring frequency; make sure the expected interval used in the audit matches current, not historical, dosing.
pearls: Use the exact structure that worked in a related paediatric audit: a shared-care guideline plus a tick-box monitoring proforma with all parameters listed together [2966].
A laboratory-generated automatic reminder is more durable than relying on either GP or hospital memory alone.
Make the responsible party for monitoring (GP vs hospital) explicit in every new thiopurine-start letter.
Track outcomes of any neutropenia detected, to show the monitoring system actually catches and acts on the risk it exists to prevent.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the laboratory system
pass: A full blood count is checked at the locally agreed interval (typically weekly for the first month, then monthly, per BNF monographs) throughout the audit period, with no gap longer than the agreed interval.

question: What proportion of adults newly diagnosed with coeliac disease have a documented discussion about pneumococcal vaccination?
why: Coeliac disease is associated with functional hyposplenism and increased pneumococcal infection risk. A related audit found overall vaccine uptake in coeliac disease was only 38.6% at baseline, improving to 49.2% with an invitation letter [9569], but no audit checks whether the vaccination discussion itself is documented at diagnosis.

standard.wording: Explain to people with coeliac disease and their family members or carers (as appropriate) that the Department of Health's Green Book recommends immunisation against pneumococcus.

population: Adults with a new diagnosis of coeliac disease in the last 12 months.
sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new diagnosis of coeliac disease.
data_source: Gastroenterology clinic letters/EPR and, where available, GP vaccination records.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a 'pneumococcal vaccination discussed' tick box with a pre-written information line to the coeliac disease diagnosis clinic letter template, sent to both the patient and the GP.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the gastroenterology-primary care interface meeting; keep the clinic letter template field if documentation improves.
evidence: [9569] a coeliac disease vaccine uptake audit found only 38.6% uptake at baseline, improving to 49.2% with a single invitation letter, showing this step needs an active system prompt rather than relying on the diagnosis conversation alone
pitfalls: The discussion may happen verbally at diagnosis but not be written down: this audit measures documentation, and should say so plainly rather than assuming the conversation never happened.
GPs, not gastroenterology, usually administer the vaccine: the audit should track the discussion (specialist's responsibility) separately from vaccine administration (usually primary care's).

Patients already vaccinated for another indication (for example, age-related pneumococcal vaccination) should still have the coeliac-specific discussion recorded, since guidance and eligibility can differ.
A generic coeliac information leaflet mentioning vaccination in passing is not the same as a documented individual discussion: define the standard clearly before starting.
pearls: A single sentence and tick box in the standard diagnosis letter, copied to the GP, is a low-effort fix that also prompts GP action.
Pair the vaccination discussion with the annual review audit above so both draw on the same diagnosis-clinic dataset.
Consider adapting the invitation-letter approach already shown to work in the library [9569] as the mechanism for actually getting patients vaccinated once discussed.
Track vaccine uptake as well as discussion rates at re-audit to confirm discussion translates into action.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from clinic letters
pass: A documented discussion about pneumococcal vaccination is recorded at, or within 3 months of, the diagnosis of coeliac disease.

question: What proportion of adults admitted with acute alcohol-related hepatitis have a documented nutritional assessment, with nutritional support started if indicated?
why: Malnutrition is near-universal in acute alcoholic hepatitis and affects survival, but no audit in the library checks whether nutritional assessment is systematically done and acted on in this specific group.

standard.wording: Assess the nutritional requirements of people with acute alcohol-related hepatitis. Offer nutritional support if needed and consider using nasogastric tube feeding.

population: Adults admitted with a clinical diagnosis of acute alcohol-related hepatitis in the last 6-12 months.
sample: 30 consecutive adults admitted with acute alcohol-related hepatitis.
data_source: Admission clerking, nursing nutritional screening records and dietitian referral system.
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add acute alcohol-related hepatitis as a trigger diagnosis for an automatic same-day dietitian referral and MUST scoring on the hepatology/gastroenterology admission bundle.
reaudit: Repeat in 6-12 months, same criteria.
close_loop: Present at the hepatology and nutrition and dietetics governance meeting; keep the automatic referral trigger if assessment completeness improves.
evidence: no audit in the library checks nutritional assessment completeness specifically in acute alcohol-related hepatitis
pitfalls: General ward MUST scoring may be completed routinely but not specifically prompt dietitian input for this high-risk group: check whether a score is acted on, not just recorded.
Nasogastric feeding can be difficult in patients with encephalopathy or agitation: a documented reason not to feed enterally should count as a valid clinical decision, not a failure.
Weekend admissions may have delayed dietitian input due to staffing: check whether delays cluster there.
Poor oral intake due to nausea or ongoing alcohol withdrawal symptoms needs separate management alongside nutrition, and should be recorded as context.
pearls: An automatic dietitian referral triggered by the diagnosis code removes reliance on the ward team remembering a nutrition-specific step amid other urgent decisions (steroids, infection screen).
Weekend and out-of-hours dietitian cover (or a clear escalation plan) is often the main practical barrier: check this with dietetics before proposing a fix.
Combine data collection with the pre-steroid infection screening audit above, since both draw from the same acute alcoholic hepatitis admission list.
Track nutritional status trends (weight, albumin) through the admission as an outcome measure at re-audit.
effort: ~15 min per case from admission and dietitian records
pass: A nutritional assessment (for example, MUST score or dietitian review) is documented within 48 hours of admission with acute alcohol-related hepatitis, with nutritional support started if indicated.
